title: Secure the software development ecosystem
question: How do development ecosystem controls prevent one compromised person, secret, dependency, or runner from becoming an untraceable production release?
scenario: A build pulls a popular package whose maintainer account was hijacked.
focalRelation: overprivileged CI token --source/build/artifact/production authority--> single compromise path separate identities and environment boundaries --cut--> lateral movement dependency/source provenance --constrains--> accepted input protected artifact plus promotion verification --constrains--> deployment rollback and rotation --contain--> incident

nodes.label: Hijacked maintainer account
nodes.detail: Compromised publisher identity capable of releasing a malicious version; popularity is not provenance.

nodes.label: Pinned dependency
nodes.detail: Explicit name, version, digest, license, owner, and usage recorded in dependency inventory.

nodes.label: Integrity and provenance check
nodes.detail: Verification of trusted publisher, signature/attestation, digest, source, and approved policy.

nodes.label: Isolated build
nodes.detail: Constrained runner without unnecessary secrets or production reach; untrusted build effects are contained.

nodes.label: Release inventory
nodes.detail: Mapping from dependency and build provenance to artifacts, deployments, customers, and exposed secrets.

nodes.label: Rollback artifact and owner
nodes.detail: Authority to freeze promotion, revoke/rotate secrets, replace artifacts, monitor, and communicate.

lanes.label: External publisher boundary
lanes.rule: Maintainer identity and package popularity do not establish trusted release.

lanes.label: Approved dependency input
lanes.rule: Pinning and inventory name exactly what the build is permitted to consume.

lanes.label: Verification boundary
lanes.rule: Integrity and provenance policy decide whether the dependency can enter the build.

lanes.label: Isolated build boundary
lanes.rule: Runner contains untrusted effects and has no unnecessary production credentials.

lanes.label: Release lineage
lanes.rule: Artifact inventory supports impact analysis and targeted response.

lanes.label: Response authority
lanes.rule: Named owner controls freeze, rebuild, rollback, secret rotation, and communication.

states.title: Case facts fixed
states.caption: A build pulls a popular package whose maintainer account was hijacked.

states.title: Controlling condition identified
states.caption: A compromised build service can undermine otherwise secure source code.

states.title: Tempting shortcut rejected
states.caption: A private repository makes source trustworthy. Repository access, review, identity, dependencies, runners, and release provenance all require controls.

states.title: Bounded action applied
states.caption: Use dependency inventory and pinning, provenance and integrity checks, review, isolated builds, monitoring, and rapid rollback. Assess impacted releases and rotate exposed secrets; trust in popularity is not provenance.

states.title: Outcome accepted with limits
states.caption: Select layered controls for a development toolchain and explain how they prevent unauthorized change, leakage, and untrusted artifacts. The case record retains the scope, owner, exceptions, and evidence used for this conclusion.

variants.label: Changed case
variants.changedFact: A CI runner has production credentials to simplify deployment.

states.title: Changed case fact isolated
states.caption: A CI runner has production credentials to simplify deployment.

states.title: Decision recomputed
states.caption: Reduce privilege, use short-lived scoped credentials and an approval/promotion boundary. A build compromise would otherwise become a production compromise.

states.title: Changed outcome verified
states.caption: The decision remains provisional until the changed dependency, enforcement result, and accountable evidence are verified.

prediction.prompt: How do development ecosystem controls prevent one compromised person, secret, dependency, or runner from becoming an untraceable production release?

options.label: A private repository makes source trustworthy.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Repository access, review, identity, dependencies, runners, and release provenance all require controls.

options.label: Keep the popular dependency because its familiar package name is enough to trust the update.
options.feedback: Incorrect: a hijacked maintainer account breaks a trust assumption. Verify publisher and artifact provenance, pin and review the exact version, assess behavior and exposure, and retain a rollback or replacement path.

options.label: Freeze the version and verify publisher, artifact, build, exposure, and rollback evidence
options.feedback: Correct for this scenario: this answer uses the displayed relation and preserves its scope. Repository access, review, identity, dependencies, runners, and release provenance all require controls.

prediction.hint: Name the controlling relationship and the point where its result must be enforced; do not rely on a label or successful prior step.

transfer.prompt: A CI runner has production credentials to simplify deployment.

options.label: Reduce privilege, use short-lived scoped credentials and an approval/promotion boundary
options.feedback: Correct. Reduce privilege, use short-lived scoped credentials and an approval/promotion boundary. A build compromise would otherwise become a production compromise.

options.label: Reuse the original conclusion because the overall control family is unchanged
options.feedback: The changed fact is “A CI runner has production credentials to simplify deployment.” Reusing the earlier conclusion skips the changed condition and the model’s publishes version considered by dependency policy relation.

options.label: Bypass the normal owner and apply a permanent broad restriction immediately
options.feedback: This bypasses the named decision owner and leaves Rollback owner unverified. Reduce privilege, use short-lived scoped credentials and an approval/promotion boundary. A build compromise would otherwise become a production compromise.

transfer.hint: Trace the changed fact to the exact decision boundary, then identify the evidence needed before the outcome can be accepted.

retry.prompt: A build pins a dependency to a mutable release tag that the publisher can move. What strengthens the trust decision?

options.label: Trust the tag because it comes from the official publisher namespace
options.feedback: A trusted namespace can still be compromised or retagged; the build needs immutable verified content.

options.label: Pin an immutable digest, verify provenance, and retain the dependency record
options.feedback: Correct. Immutable identity and provenance make later reproduction and incident tracing possible.

options.label: Copy the package into an internal folder without recording origin or digest
options.feedback: Relocation alone does not establish provenance, integrity, or update accountability.

retry.hint: A readable version label is not necessarily an immutable identity.

takeaway: Use dependency inventory and pinning, provenance and integrity checks, review, isolated builds, monitoring, and rapid rollback.
assumptions: The scenario is a bounded application of the canonical unit, not a universal threshold, legal conclusion, or vendor prescription.
Directed edges carry only their printed relation; proximity and shared color do not imply ownership, authorization, or chronology.
Acceptance applies only to the stated scope and retained evidence; unknown or excluded conditions remain explicit.

treatmentDispositions.rationale: Implemented in 5 stable boundary states: Hijacked maintainer account publishes version considered by dependency policy Pinned dependency; Pinned dependency is verified against pin, digest, and provenance Integrity and provenance check. The model keeps Hijacked maintainer account, Pinned dependency, Integrity and provenance check, Isolated build, Release inventory, Rollback owner distinct. Its changed case is “A CI runner has production credentials to simplify deployment.” and every option returns to a named repair state.
